snp1.2:1.1: Lit. “I am cooked rice and fresh milk.” However this would be nonsensical if translated literally, so the implied meaning appears to be ownership - ie, that Dhaniya has a supply of food in his hut.
snp1.2:1.3: The term _mahī_ simply means “large, great” and was the name of one of the major rivers in the region; it was one of the rivers regarded as innately holy by many of the non-Buddhist religions of the time.
snp1.2:2.1: The Buddha is making a pun that is impossible to capture in translation. _Pakkodana_ (cooked rice) and _akkodhana_ (no anger), and _khīra_ (milk) and _khila_ (corruption).
snp1.2:2.3: This is presumably to indicate that the Buddha can stay at any place but is not bound to that place; and is probably also a subtle indication that he places no particular spiritual significance on the supposedly holy river Mahī.
snp1.2:2.4: The imagery of the “extinguished fire” is clearly a reference to awakening (ie, the fires of defilement and delusion have been extinguished). The “open hut” (_vivaṭā kuṭi_) may be referring to the mind being clear and alert, as the word _vivaṭa_ has that meaning elsewhere in the suttas.
snp1.2:15.2: This indicates that he decided to become a monk.
